PET CUSTODY AND CARE AGREEMENT
Prepared for Jane Doe · John Smith

PARTIES AND THE PET
This Pet Custody and Care Agreement is entered into between Jane Doe and John Smith (together, the "Co-Owners"), effective January 1, 2026, concerning a 4-year-old golden retriever named Max (the "Pet"), in which both Co-Owners have an ownership interest. This agreement applies regardless of whether Jane Doe and John Smith are married to each other, registered domestic partners, dating partners, roommates, or co-owners under some other arrangement, and regardless of whether either of them has filed, or ever files, a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, legal separation, or dissolution of a registered domestic partnership involving the other.

☐ Jane Doe and John Smith acquired the Pet together.
☐ Jane Doe originally acquired the Pet.
☐ John Smith originally acquired the Pet.
☐ Other: _______________________________________________.

Both Co-Owners agree that each has an ownership interest in the Pet as described above, and that this agreement governs how they will share possession, care, and expenses for the Pet going forward.

POSSESSION SCHEDULE
The Pet will primarily reside with: ☐ Jane Doe ☐ John Smith ☐ alternating between both Co-Owners on the following schedule: _______________________________________________.

Handoffs of the Pet will take place at _______________________________________________ (location), on the following schedule: _______________________________________________, with _______________________________________________ responsible for transporting the Pet to each handoff unless the Co-Owners agree otherwise for a particular exchange.

Each Co-Owner will give the other Co-Owner at least _______ days' notice before a planned absence of more than _______ days that falls during that Co-Owner's scheduled time with the Pet, and the Co-Owners will agree in advance on care arrangements for the Pet during that absence.

EXPENSES AND VETERINARY DECISIONS
Routine expenses for the Pet's food, grooming, licensing, and supplies will be paid: ☐ equally by Jane Doe and John Smith ☐ by whichever Co-Owner has possession of the Pet when the expense is incurred ☐ as follows: _______________________________________________.

A veterinary expense of more than $_______ for a single visit or procedure requires both Co-Owners' agreement in advance, except that, in a genuine emergency, the Co-Owner who has possession of the Pet at the time may authorize necessary emergency treatment without the other Co-Owner's prior agreement. The Co-Owners will divide a veterinary expense incurred under this paragraph: ☐ equally ☐ as follows: _______________________________________________.

Either Co-Owner may take the Pet to a veterinarian of that Co-Owner's choosing during that Co-Owner's own scheduled time with the Pet. Each Co-Owner will, on the other Co-Owner's request, share the Pet's medical records and the name and contact information of any veterinarian who has treated the Pet.

A PRIVATE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CO-OWNERS IS NOT A FAMILY CODE SECTION 2605 COURT ORDER
California's Family Code gives a court the authority, in a pending case, to enter an order for a pet animal's interim care and to assign a pet animal's ownership under Family Code section 2605, but that section sits within the part of the Family Code that, by its own terms, "applies to a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, for nullity of marriage, or for legal separation of the parties." Only a married spouse can bring that kind of proceeding against the other spouse. A registered domestic partnership exists only once "both persons file a Declaration of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State" — it is not created simply because two adults share a household, a relationship, or a pet — but once registered, domestic partners "shall have the same rights, protections, and benefits, and shall be subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties under law...as are granted to and imposed upon spouses," which extends the dissolution and legal-separation framework section 2605 sits within to registered domestic partners as well. Jane Doe and John Smith entering into this agreement — whether or not either of them is married to, or a registered domestic partner of, the other, and whether or not a dissolution or legal-separation proceeding between them is pending or ever filed — does not request, grant, or constitute a section 2605 order. This agreement is instead an ordinary contract between Jane Doe and John Smith over possession and care of the Pet, which they agree they both own an interest in, and it does not depend on either Co-Owner ever qualifying for, or using, the dissolution or legal-separation mechanism section 2605 operates within.

[This clause's source hasn't been independently confirmed against the government's own primary text yet (it's sourced to a secondary copy, or hasn't been checked at all). Treat the quote below as a starting point, not a confirmed fact, until it is.]
  "This part applies to a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, for nullity of marriage, or for legal separation of the parties."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2000 (law.onecle.com text), Family Code Part 2000's own scope provision, naming only marriage-dissolution, nullity, and legal-separation proceedings (https://law.onecle.com/california/family/2000.html)
  "(a) Domestic partners are two adults who have chosen to share one another’s lives in an intimate and committed relationship of mutual caring.
(b) A domestic partnership shall be established in California when both persons file a Declaration of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State pursuant to this division, and, at the time of filing, all of the following requirements are met:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 297(a)-(b) (law.onecle.com text), the statutory definition of a domestic partnership, requiring an affirmative filing with the Secretary of State (https://law.onecle.com/california/family/297.html)
  "(a) Registered domestic partners shall have the same rights, protections, and benefits, and shall be subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties under law, whether they derive from statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, or any other provisions or sources of law, as are granted to and imposed upon spouses."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(a) (law.onecle.com text), registered domestic partners' statutory entitlement to the same rights and obligations as spouses generally (https://law.onecle.com/california/family/297.5.html)
  Known gap: Family Code section 2605's own text is not independently quoted in this clause. Every attempt this session to fetch it directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov — the Legislature's own site, and this corpus's standard primary source for California statutes — returned an HTTP 403 Cloudflare bot-management challenge page ("Just a moment...") instead of the statute, on repeated tries with different User-Agent strings and through this project's web-fetch tool as well as direct HTTPS requests; the site is evidently network-blocked in this environment. This document's usual mirror fallback, law.onecle.com, does not carry section 2605 at all (its California Family Code page for section 2605 returns HTTP 404) — consistent with that mirror's own footer date ("Last modified: October 25, 2018") predating section 2605's January 1, 2019 operative date. This corpus's separate, already-verified pet_animal_custody_ownership_info_sheet document (clauses petcustody_interim_care_order, petcustody_ownership_assignment_standard, and petcustody_pet_animal_definition, checked 2026-09-06 directly against leginfo) is the existing record of section 2605's own operative text, including that it reaches only a "pet animal" that "is community property," and this document does not re-verify that text. What this clause instead independently verifies, all freshly fetched this session from law.onecle.com (sourceClass: mirror, for the same leginfo-blocked reason) are: that Family Code Part 2000's own scope provision names only marriage-dissolution, nullity, and legal-separation proceedings; that a domestic partnership requires an affirmative Secretary of State filing under section 297(a)-(b); and that section 297.5(a) extends spousal rights and obligations to a partnership once registered. As a cross-check on the onecle mirror's continued reliability, this session's freshly fetched text of a different section the corpus already verified against leginfo — Family Code section 2550 — matched that primary-sourced quote word for word, which is some evidence (not a guarantee) that onecle's mirror text for these older, frequently cited Family Code provisions remains current. This clause does not address, and did not research, whether a court exercising section 2605 authority in an actual proceeding would treat a prior private agreement like this one as controlling, as one relevant consideration, or as not controlling at all; nor does it address whether Jane Doe or John Smith's interest in the Pet is community, quasi-community, or separate property, which this agreement does not itself determine.

A PET'S LEGAL "VALUE" IS ITS ECONOMIC VALUE, NOT ITS SENTIMENTAL VALUE
When California law measures what a particular piece of property is worth to its owner for money-damages purposes, it recognizes a "peculiar value" concept: Civil Code section 3355 provides that “[w]here certain property has a peculiar value to a person recovering damages for deprivation thereof, or injury thereto, that may be deemed to be its value against one who had notice thereof before incurring a liability to damages in respect thereof, or against a willful wrongdoer.” Applying that statute to a dog's death from alleged veterinary malpractice, a California Court of Appeal held that “[p]eculiar value under Civil Code section 3355 refers to a property’s unique economic value, not its sentimental or emotional value” — so a dog's pedigree, breeding record, or ability to win competitions can count toward its "peculiar value," but how deeply its owner loves it cannot. If a dispute between Jane Doe and John Smith over the Pet were ever litigated as a claim for money damages rather than as a request for the Pet itself, this is the measure of value a California court has applied: the Pet's economic worth, not either Co-Owner's emotional attachment to it.

[This clause's source hasn't been independently confirmed against the government's own primary text yet (it's sourced to a secondary copy, or hasn't been checked at all). Treat the quote below as a starting point, not a confirmed fact, until it is.]
  "Civil Code section 3355 provides: “Where certain property has a peculiar value to a person recovering damages for deprivation thereof, or injury thereto, that may be deemed to be its value against one who had notice thereof before incurring a liability to damages in respect thereof, or against a willful wrongdoer.”"
  — McMahon v. Craig, 176 Cal.App.4th 1502, 1518 (2009) (opinion text via CourtListener), California Court of Appeal, quoting Civil Code section 3355's "peculiar value" measure of damages (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2255876/mcmahon-v-craig/)
  "Peculiar value under Civil Code section 3355 refers to a property’s unique economic value, not its sentimental or emotional value."
  — McMahon v. Craig, 176 Cal.App.4th 1502, 1518-1519 (2009) (opinion text via CourtListener), California Court of Appeal, holding that "peculiar value" is economic, not sentimental (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2255876/mcmahon-v-craig/)
  Known gap: Both quotations are read directly from the opinion text of McMahon v. Craig (2009) 176 Cal.App.4th 1502, 1518, fetched fresh this session via CourtListener (opinion id 2255876) — a primary court-opinion source, not a mirror, and not leginfo (so the Cloudflare-blocking problem described in this document's other authority clauses does not affect this one). McMahon is a single, published Fourth District Court of Appeal decision about a dog's death from alleged veterinary malpractice; it is not a case about a dispute between two co-owners over sharing a living pet's possession, and no broader search of other California appellate districts or the California Supreme Court was done to confirm no later decision has limited or distinguished its "peculiar value" holding. The two older cases McMahon itself discusses and quotes for how "peculiar value" has been applied to an animal — Roos v. Loeser (1919) 41 Cal.App. 782 and King v. Karpe (1959) 170 Cal.App.2d 344 — were not independently fetched and verified for this document; this clause relies only on McMahon's own direct quotation of the statute and its own stated holding, not on this document's independent reading of those two older opinions. This clause does not address, and did not research, what remedy (money damages, return of the Pet itself, or something else) a court would actually order in a dispute between co-owners over continued possession of a shared pet — it addresses only how a California court has measured a pet's money value when money damages are the relief sought.

WHY THIS AGREEMENT IS IN WRITING
Under California law, a "contract is an agreement to do or not to do a certain thing," and it is essential to a contract's existence that there be "[p]arties capable of contracting," "[t]heir consent," "[a] lawful object," and "[a] sufficient cause or consideration." Separately, "[a]n agreement that by its terms is not to be performed within a year from the making thereof" is invalid "unless [it], or some note or memorandum thereof, [is] in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged or by the party's agent." An ongoing arrangement for sharing a pet's possession and expenses, with no end date or an end date more than a year away, is the kind of agreement this writing requirement reaches. Putting this agreement in writing and having Jane Doe and John Smith both sign it is what keeps an arrangement of that kind enforceable as a contract for as long as it continues.

[This clause's source hasn't been independently confirmed against the government's own primary text yet (it's sourced to a secondary copy, or hasn't been checked at all). Treat the quote below as a starting point, not a confirmed fact, until it is.]
  "A contract is an agreement to do or not to do a certain thing."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1549 (law.onecle.com text), the statutory definition of a contract (https://law.onecle.com/california/civil/1549.html)
  "It is essential to the existence of a contract that there should be:
1. Parties capable of contracting;
2. Their consent;
3. A lawful object; and,
4. A sufficient cause or consideration."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1550 (law.onecle.com text), the essential elements of a contract (https://law.onecle.com/california/civil/1550.html)
  "(a) The following contracts are invalid, unless they, or some note or memorandum thereof, are in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged or by the party’s agent:
(1) An agreement that by its terms is not to be performed within a year from the making thereof."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1624(a)(1) (law.onecle.com text), the statute of frauds requirement for an agreement not to be performed within a year (https://law.onecle.com/california/civil/1624.html)
  Known gap: These Civil Code quotations (sections 1549, 1550, and 1624(a)(1)) were fetched fresh this session from law.onecle.com, not from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, which returned a Cloudflare bot-management challenge page on every attempt this session (described in more detail in this document's petagreement_private_contract_outside_family_code_2605 clause). All three sections date to California's original 1872 enactment of the Civil Code and, on this document's own check, have not been renumbered or repealed; this document did not independently confirm whether section 1624 (last amended, per onecle's own text, in 2014) has been further amended since the mirror's own last-modified date of October 25, 2018. This clause does not address whether a shorter-term or month-to-month version of this kind of agreement would independently require a writing under section 1624(a)(1) — that depends on the actual term agreed to — nor did it research partial performance, promissory estoppel, or any other doctrine that can make an otherwise-unwritten agreement enforceable despite section 1624; those doctrines exist in California contract law generally but are not confirmed here.

IF A CO-OWNER CAN NO LONGER KEEP THE PET
If Jane Doe or John Smith decides that Co-Owner can no longer keep or share possession of the Pet going forward — because of a move, a change in housing, a change in finances, a change in health, or any other reason — that Co-Owner will notify the other Co-Owner in writing at least _______ days before the change takes effect, to the extent the circumstances allow that much notice.

Before placing the Pet with a new owner, surrendering the Pet to a shelter or rescue organization, or otherwise permanently transferring the Pet to anyone other than Jane Doe or John Smith, the Co-Owner seeking to do so will first offer the other Co-Owner the opportunity to take over sole ownership and possession of the Pet. If the other Co-Owner accepts that offer within _______ days of the offer, the Pet transfers to that Co-Owner's sole ownership on whatever further terms the Co-Owners agree to at that time, and this agreement terminates as to the Pet.

Neither Co-Owner will have the Pet euthanized except on a licensed veterinarian's recommendation that euthanasia is necessary for the Pet's health or welfare, or with the other Co-Owner's written agreement.

A REMEDY IF A CO-OWNER DOES NOT RETURN THE PET
California law lets a person compel someone else who has "possession or control of a particular article of personal property," and who is "not [its] owner," to "specifically deliver it to the person entitled to its immediate possession." More generally, "the specific performance of an obligation may be compelled" — an order that a party actually do what they agreed to do, rather than only pay money damages for not doing it — "[e]xcept as otherwise provided" elsewhere in that chapter of the Civil Code. Because a particular pet is not a fungible item that money can simply substitute for with an equivalent replacement, a request to compel a Co-Owner to actually hand over the Pet, rather than only pay its monetary value, draws on these general California property and contract remedies.

[This clause's source hasn't been independently confirmed against the government's own primary text yet (it's sourced to a secondary copy, or hasn't been checked at all). Treat the quote below as a starting point, not a confirmed fact, until it is.]
  "Any person having the possession or control of a particular article of personal property, of which he is not the owner, may be compelled specifically to deliver it to the person entitled to its immediate possession."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3380 (law.onecle.com text), compelling specific delivery of a particular article of personal property to the person entitled to its immediate possession (https://law.onecle.com/california/civil/3380.html)
  "Except as otherwise provided in this Article, the specific performance of an obligation may be compelled."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3384 (law.onecle.com text), the general availability of specific performance of an obligation (https://law.onecle.com/california/civil/3384.html)
  Known gap: Both quotations were fetched fresh this session from law.onecle.com (Civil Code sections 3380 and 3384), for the same leginfo-blocking reason described in this document's other authority clauses; both sections date to an 1873-74 Civil Code amendment and, on this document's own check, have not been renumbered or repealed. Section 3380's own text addresses a person in possession or control of a particular article of personal property "of which he is not the owner" — it does not, on its face, address a dispute between two people who are each already a co-owner of the same property, which is exactly Jane Doe and John Smith's situation under this agreement with respect to the Pet. No California case law was independently researched for this clause to confirm whether, or how, a court applies section 3380's non-owner framing to a dispute between co-owners, or whether a court would order the Pet delivered to one Co-Owner rather than award money damages in a dispute between Jane Doe and John Smith specifically. This clause identifies the general statutory remedy that exists for a particular article of personal property and the open question this agreement's co-ownership setting raises for it; it does not resolve that question or predict how a court would rule.

SIGNATURES
Signed:

Jane Doe: _________________________ Date: _________________________

John Smith: _________________________ Date: _________________________

Signed at San Diego, California on January 1, 2026.

—

If Jane Doe or John Smith decides that Co-Owner can no longer keep or share possession of the Pet going forward — because of a move, a change in housing, a change in finances, a change in health, or any other reason — that Co-Owner will notify the other Co-Owner in writing at least _______ days before the change takes effect, to the extent the circumstances allow that much notice.

Before placing the Pet with a new owner, surrendering the Pet to a shelter or rescue organization, or otherwise permanently transferring the Pet to anyone other than Jane Doe or John Smith, the Co-Owner seeking to do so will first offer the other Co-Owner the opportunity to take over sole ownership and possession of the Pet. If the other Co-Owner accepts that offer within _______ days of the offer, the Pet transfers to that Co-Owner's sole ownership on whatever further terms the Co-Owners agree to at that time, and this agreement terminates as to the Pet.

Neither Co-Owner will have the Pet euthanized except on a licensed veterinarian's recommendation that euthanasia is necessary for the Pet's health or welfare, or with the other Co-Owner's written agreement.

California law lets a person compel someone else who has "possession or control of a particular article of personal property," and who is "not [its] owner," to "specifically deliver it to the person entitled to its immediate possession." More generally, "the specific performance of an obligation may be compelled" — an order that a party actually do what they agreed to do, rather than only pay money damages for not doing it — "[e]xcept as otherwise provided" elsewhere in that chapter of the Civil Code. Because a particular pet is not a fungible item that money can simply substitute for with an equivalent replacement, a request to compel a Co-Owner to actually hand over the Pet, rather than only pay its monetary value, draws on these general California property and contract remedies.

citations.cite: compelling specific delivery of a particular article of personal property to the person entitled to its immediate possession
citations.quote: Any person having the possession or control of a particular article of personal property, of which he is not the owner, may be compelled specifically to deliver it to the person entitled to its immediate possession.

citations.cite: the general availability of specific performance of an obligation
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this Article, the specific performance of an obligation may be compelled.

expectedJSON.gap: Both quotations were fetched fresh this session from law.onecle.com (Civil Code sections 3380 and 3384), for the same leginfo-blocking reason described in this document's other authority clauses; both sections date to an 1873-74 Civil Code amendment and, on this document's own check, have not been renumbered or repealed. Section 3380's own text addresses a person in possession or control of a particular article of personal property "of which he is not the owner" — it does not, on its face, address a dispute between two people who are each already a co-owner of the same property, which is exactly Jane Doe and John Smith's situation under this agreement with respect to the Pet. No California case law was independently researched for this clause to confirm whether, or how, a court applies section 3380's non-owner framing to a dispute between co-owners, or whether a court would order the Pet delivered to one Co-Owner rather than award money damages in a dispute between Jane Doe and John Smith specifically. This clause identifies the general statutory remedy that exists for a particular article of personal property and the open question this agreement's co-ownership setting raises for it; it does not resolve that question or predict how a court would rule.
